warmup.q: A payment service counts retries with private volatile int retries; and retries++ from 8 request threads. After 800,000 retries, what does retries hold?
options: Exactly 800,000, because volatile makes every access go straight to memory
Exactly 800,000 on x86, less on ARM
It won't compile: ++ isn't allowed on a volatile field
warmup.why: retries++ is a read, an add and a write. volatile makes each of those visible and ordered, but two threads can still read the same value and both write value + 1. The first option is the classic belief: "goes to memory" is true, and it doesn't make the three steps one.

sections.h: volatile gives you visibility and ordering
sections.html:
Declaring a field volatile gets you three things, and you've already used two of them in this track.

Visibility. A volatile read sees the latest volatile write to that field. The JIT can't keep the value in a register or hoist the read out of a loop. That was the stop flag in lesson 1 of this track.

Ordering. A volatile write is a release: plain writes that come before it in program order can't move after it. A volatile read is an acquire: plain reads after it can't move before it. That's the piggybacking from lesson 2 of this track.

Java
config = load();        // plain write: stays before the volatile write
version = 42;           // volatile write (release)

if (version == 42) {    // volatile read (acquire), in another thread
    use(config);        // plain read: stays after it, and sees the config
}
Kotlin
config = load()         // plain write: stays before the volatile write
version = 42            // @Volatile write (release)

if (version == 42) {    // @Volatile read (acquire), in another thread
    use(config)         // plain read: stays after it, and sees the config
}

One order for all volatile accesses. Every thread agrees on a single order of all volatile reads and writes. That's what forbids the store-buffering outcome from lesson 1 of this track, where both threads read 0. Acquire and release alone don't forbid it; lesson 6 of this track shows the difference.

The ordering only helps threads that both use the volatile. If thread A writes a volatile x and thread B writes a plain y, B's write can still sit in its store buffer while B reads x. The try-it below measures this.

The cost is lower than people fear. On x86 a volatile read compiles to an ordinary load; the only cost is that the JIT can't optimize around it. A volatile write costs more, because HotSpot follows it with an instruction that drains the store buffer. On ARM, HotSpot uses dedicated load-acquire and store-release instructions. For a flag read on every request, the price is noise next to one database call.

try.title: Make only one side volatile
steps: Read HalfVolatileDemo. It runs the store-buffering test three ways: no volatile, only x volatile, and both volatile.
Predict the middle column before you run: does one volatile field save both threads?
Run it with the command below.

code.title: HalfVolatileDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l03; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track, three ways: no volatile, only x volatile, * both fields volatile. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * Counts the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class HalfVolatileDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class XOnly { volatile int x; int y; } static final class Both { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 in plain: %,7d only x volatile: %,7d both volatile: %,d%n", run, plain(), xOnly(), both()); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Plain[] s = new Plain[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int xOnly() throws InterruptedException { XOnly[] s = new XOnly[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new XOnly(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int both() throws InterruptedException { Both[] s = new Both[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Both(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads, in lockstep batches so they overlap. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } }

alt.title: HalfVolatileDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l03 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track, three ways: no @Volatile, only x @Volatile, * both fields @Volatile. Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. * Counts the trials where both threads read 0. */ private class NoVolatile { var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class XVolatile { @Volatile var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class BothVolatile { @Volatile var x = 0; @Volatile var y = 0 } private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 19 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 in plain: %,7d only x @Volatile: %,7d both @Volatile: %,d" .format(run, plain(), xOnly(), both())) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { NoVolatile() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun xOnly(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { XVolatile() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun both(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { BothVolatile() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads, in lockstep batches so they overlap. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 }

try.expect: Plain fields show both threads reading 0 in a large share of trials. With only x volatile the count drops but stays well above zero (tens of thousands here): thread B's write to plain y can still wait in its store buffer while it reads x. Only when both fields are volatile does the count go to 0.

sections.h: volatile does not make count++ atomic
sections.html:
Here's the bug from the warm-up:

Java
private volatile int retries;

void onRetry() {
    retries++;   // read, add one, write: three steps
}
Kotlin
@Volatile private var retries = 0

fun onRetry() {
    retries++    // read, add one, write: three steps
}

volatile makes the read fresh and the write visible. It does nothing about the gap between them. Two threads read 41, both add one, both write 42. Each of those six accesses was perfectly volatile.

The research for this track measured it: 4 threads each ran v++ a million times on a static volatile int, and the total came out at 3,681,731 instead of 4,000,000. The same run with a plain int came out at 3,997,394. The plain counter looked less wrong in that run, and that proves nothing: the JIT can batch plain increments in a register, which changes how many get lost. Runs for this lesson saw the order flip. Both are broken.

The fix is a single step that reads and writes as one:

Java
private final AtomicInteger retries = new AtomicInteger();

void onRetry() {
    retries.incrementAndGet();   // one atomic read-modify-write
}
Kotlin
private val retries = AtomicInteger()

fun onRetry() {
    retries.incrementAndGet()    // one atomic read-modify-write
}

For a counter that many threads hit hard and that you only read now and then (metrics), LongAdder is faster still. A lock works too, and it's the only choice once the update touches more than one field.

The same trap hides in any compound action on a volatile: if (balance >= amount) balance -= amount, max = Math.max(max, x), if (state == OPEN) state = CLOSED. Every one of them reads, decides and writes as separate steps.

try.title: Count four ways
steps: Read VolatileCounterDemo. Four threads each add 1,000,000 to a plain counter, a volatile counter, an AtomicInteger and a LongAdder.
Predict which of the four reach 4,000,000, and whether volatile loses fewer updates than plain.
Run it twice with the command below and compare the runs.

code.title: VolatileCounterDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l03; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter. Which ones add up? */ public class VolatileCounterDemo { static int plain; static volatile int vol; static final AtomicInteger atomic = new AtomicInteger(); static final LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); static final int THREADS = 4, PER_THREAD = 1_000_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("plain int", () -> plain++); run("volatile int", () -> vol++); run("AtomicInteger", atomic::incrementAndGet); run("LongAdder", adder::increment); System.out.printf("expected %,d each%n", THREADS * PER_THREAD); System.out.printf("plain %,d volatile %,d atomic %,d adder %,d%n", plain, vol, atomic.get(), adder.sum()); } static void run(String name, Runnable increment) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] ts = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int t = 0; t < THREADS; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) increment.run(); }, name + "-" + t); } for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); // join: the final reads in main see every thread's writes } }

alt.title: VolatileCounterDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l03 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var plain = 0 @Volatile private var vol = 0 private val atomic = AtomicInteger() private val adder = LongAdder() private const val THREADS = 4 private const val PER_THREAD = 1_000_000 /** Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter. Which ones add up? */ fun main() { hammer("plain Int") { plain++ } hammer("@Volatile Int") { vol++ } hammer("AtomicInteger") { atomic.incrementAndGet() } hammer("LongAdder") { adder.increment() } println("expected %,d each".format(THREADS * PER_THREAD)) println("plain %,d @Volatile %,d atomic %,d adder %,d".format(plain, vol, atomic.get(), adder.sum())) } private fun hammer(name: String, increment: () -> Unit) { val ts = List(THREADS) { t -> thread(name = "$name-$t") { repeat(PER_THREAD) { increment() } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } // join: the final reads in main see every thread's writes }

try.expect: The atomic and the adder print exactly 4,000,000 every time. Plain and volatile both come out short, often by hundreds of thousands, and which of the two loses more changes from run to run. The volatile counter is not "more correct"; it's wrong in a different pattern.

sections.h: When volatile is enough, and when you need more
sections.html:
Volatile is the right tool when all of these hold:

  • Only one thread writes the field, or every write sets a value that doesn't depend on the current one.
  • The field isn't part of a rule that involves other fields.
  • Readers need the latest value, nothing more.

That covers more fields than you'd think: a shutdown flag, a status that one callback thread moves forward, a last-heartbeat timestamp, a Kafka lag gauge that one poller updates. It also covers a reference to an immutable object that one thread replaces whole, such as a rate table refreshed every minute. Readers grab the current table with one volatile read, and the table itself never changes.

The moment a decision needs a read, then a write based on what you read, volatile stops being enough. One variable with many writers takes an atomic class (incrementAndGet, compareAndSet, updateAndGet). Several variables that must change together, or a check that spans them, take a lock.

Shape of the field Tool
One writer, readers need the latest value volatile
Many writers, one variable, read-modify-write AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, LongAdder
Two or more fields under one rule a lock around every read and write
A whole immutable object, replaced now and then a volatile reference or AtomicReference

One mixed pattern is worth knowing. If writes are rare and reads are hot, make the writes synchronized and the field volatile. Writers exclude each other through the lock, so += is safe, and readers pay only for one volatile read.

Java
private volatile long balance;

public long balance() { return balance; }                          // readers: one volatile read
public synchronized void apply(long delta) { balance += delta; }   // writers: the lock makes += safe
Kotlin
@Volatile private var balance = 0L

fun balance(): Long = balance                                 // readers: one volatile read
@Synchronized fun apply(delta: Long) { balance += delta }     // writers: the lock makes += safe

The simulator shows the limit. Both fields are volatile, yet the capture-once rule fails.

sim.title: Capture once, with every field volatile
sim.intro: Both fields are volatile. status 1 means AUTHORIZED and 2 means CAPTURED, and a payment may be captured once. You are the scheduler: can you capture it twice?

goal.say: Both threads passed the check before either set CAPTURED: 130 captured on a 100 authorization. Every read and write was volatile and visible at once. The check and the act were still two steps.

try.title: Pick the tool
steps: Choose volatile, an atomic or a lock for each field, and say why in one line.
(a) boolean maintenanceMode, flipped by an admin endpoint, read by every request.
(b) int inFlight, incremented when a request starts and decremented when it ends, by request threads.
(c) long dailyLimitCents and long spentTodayCents, checked together before each authorization.
(d) Map<String, Rule> rules, replaced every minute by a refresher thread with a new map that nobody modifies.
try.expect: (a) volatile: writes don't depend on the old value. (b) An atomic (AtomicInteger or LongAdder): many writers doing read-modify-write. (c) A lock: one rule spans two fields and needs check-then-act. (d) A volatile reference to an immutable map, built with Map.copyOf before it is published.

sections.h: What volatile covers: one variable, all 64 bits, and nothing behind it
sections.html:
Three details trip people up once the basics are clear.

First, long and double. The JLS (section 17.7) lets the JVM treat a write to a non-volatile long or double as two separate 32-bit writes. A racing reader could then see the high half of one value and the low half of another. Writes and reads of volatile long and double are always atomic, and so are references and every type of 32 bits or less. The jcstress suite shows torn longs on a 32-bit x86 JVM: a reader saw -4294967296 and 4294967295 when the only values ever written were 0 and -1. 64-bit HotSpot writes a long in one instruction, so you won't see tearing there, but the spec doesn't promise it. In practice this rarely matters on its own: a long that two threads share needs volatile for visibility anyway, and you get atomicity with it.

Second, a volatile reference covers the reference and nothing inside the object. Writing fees.add(f) to a volatile List<Fee> fees is not a volatile write. It's a call on whatever list the field points to, with no edge for readers and no protection for the list. Replace the whole object instead:

Java
private volatile List<Fee> fees = List.of();   // volatile covers the reference only

void replaceFees(List<Fee> fresh) {
    fees = List.copyOf(fresh);                 // one volatile write of an immutable list
}
Kotlin
@Volatile private var fees: List<Fee> = emptyList()   // @Volatile covers the reference only

fun replaceFees(fresh: List<Fee>) {
    fees = fresh.toList()                              // one write of a copy nobody else holds
}

The jcstress sample AdvancedJMM_05_MisplacedVolatile shows the cost of getting this wrong. A volatile field held a holder object, but the new value went into a plain field inside the holder. On AArch64 a reader saw the new object's field still at 0 in 553 samples.

Third, arrays. A volatile long[] makes the array reference volatile and leaves every element plain. For volatile elements, use AtomicLongArray, AtomicIntegerArray or AtomicReferenceArray:

Java
class BalanceBoard {
    private volatile long[] balances = new long[16];               // volatile reference, plain elements
    private final AtomicLongArray safe = new AtomicLongArray(16);   // each element acts like a volatile

    void post(int account, long cents) {
        balances[account] = cents;   // plain element write: no edge for readers
        safe.set(account, cents);    // volatile element write: readers of safe.get() see it
    }
}
Kotlin
class BalanceBoard {
    @Volatile private var balances = LongArray(16)   // volatile reference, plain elements
    private val safe = AtomicLongArray(16)           // each element acts like a volatile

    fun post(account: Int, cents: Long) {
        balances[account] = cents   // plain element write: no edge for readers
        safe.set(account, cents)    // volatile element write: readers of safe.get() see it
    }
}

analogy: A volatile field is a number on the office whiteboard instead of in someone's notebook. Everyone reads the board directly, nobody copies it to a private note, and everyone sees the changes in the same order. But two people can still walk up, both read 41, both go back to their desks to add one, and both write 42. The board was always current; the update just wasn't one step. The analogy is weak in one place: a real whiteboard has no rule about the notes you wrote before updating it. A volatile write does: everything you wrote before it becomes visible to whoever reads the new value.
world: Look at hand-rolled circuit breakers and rate limiters in your services. A common shape is volatile int failures with failures++ on every issuer timeout and if (failures > 5) open() right after. Under a burst of timeouts from the card issuer, increments get lost and the breaker opens late, exactly when it should be fastest. Libraries such as SmallRye Fault Tolerance use proper atomics or locks for this; copy them, or use them. The good uses of volatile are just as common: a volatile RateTable current that a scheduler replaces every minute, a volatile boolean draining that a Quarkus shutdown observer sets, a volatile long lastPollMillis for a Kafka liveness check.
mistake: The most common mistake is reaching for volatile as the general fix for "thread-safety": a field is shared, so it gets the keyword. That works for flags and single-writer values, and quietly fails for counters, check-then-act and any rule that spans two fields, because volatile makes each access visible and ordered without joining them into one step. Before adding volatile, ask who writes the field and whether the new value depends on the old one. If several threads write, or the write depends on a read, use an atomic or a lock.

compare.title: A volatile snapshot reference in Java and Kotlin

java.title: FraudRules.java
java.html: public class FraudRules { // replaced whole, never mutated: one volatile read gives a consistent snapshot private volatile Map<String, Rule> rules = Map.of(); // one refresher thread public void refresh(Map<String, Rule> fresh) { rules = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build first, then publish with one volatile write } // many request threads public Rule ruleFor(String merchantCategory) { return rules.get(merchantCategory); } }

kotlin.title: FraudRules.kt
kotlin.html: class FraudRules { // replaced whole, never mutated: one volatile read gives a consistent snapshot @Volatile private var rules: Map<String, Rule> = emptyMap() // one refresher thread fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, Rule>) { rules = fresh.toMap() // a private copy, then publish with one volatile write } // many request threads fun ruleFor(merchantCategory: String): Rule? = rules[merchantCategory] }

compare.note: The pattern is identical: build a new map, publish it with one volatile write, and never touch it again. The difference is in the copy. Java's Map.copyOf returns a truly unmodifiable map (and rejects nulls). Kotlin's Map type is only a read-only view, so the safety comes from toMap() making a fresh LinkedHashMap that no other code holds. If you passed the caller's map straight through, someone with a MutableMap reference could still change it under the readers.

worked.title: Choose the tools for a circuit breaker

steps.say: A breaker in front of a card issuer opens after 5 failures in a row. Request threads call onFailure and onSuccess, and check allowRequest before each call. Every field is volatile. For each field, ask: who writes it, and does the write depend on a read?
steps.code: class IssuerBreaker { private volatile int consecutiveFailures; // written by request threads private volatile long openedAtMillis; // 0 means closed void onFailure(long now) { consecutiveFailures++; // 1. read-modify-write if (consecutiveFailures >= 5 && openedAtMillis == 0) openedAtMillis = now; // 2. check-then-act } void onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures = 0; } boolean allowRequest(long now) { long opened = openedAtMillis; return opened == 0 || now - opened > 30_000; } }

alt.html: class IssuerBreaker { @Volatile private var consecutiveFailures = 0 // written by request threads @Volatile private var openedAtMillis = 0L // 0 means closed fun onFailure(now: Long) { consecutiveFailures++ // 1. read-modify-write if (consecutiveFailures >= 5 && openedAtMillis == 0L) openedAtMillis = now // 2. check-then-act } fun onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures = 0 } fun allowRequest(now: Long): Boolean { val opened = openedAtMillis return opened == 0L || now - opened > 30_000 } }

steps.say: consecutiveFailures has many writers, and ++ depends on a read, so increments get lost and the breaker opens late. Line 2 reads the counter again, separately, and then reads and writes openedAtMillis: two threads can both see 5 and both set the time. openedAtMillis itself is fine as volatile for the readers in allowRequest, which need one value and nothing else.

Make the counter atomic and decide on the value it returns. Each incrementAndGet returns a different number, so only one thread sees exactly 5 for each run of failures, and only that thread opens the breaker.
steps.code: class IssuerBreaker { private final AtomicInteger consecutiveFailures = new AtomicInteger(); // 1. many writers: atomic private volatile long openedAtMillis; // 2. readers need one value: volatile void onFailure(long now) { int n = consecutiveFailures.incrementAndGet(); // 3. one atomic step, and keep the result if (n == 5) openedAtMillis = now; // 4. only one thread sees n == 5 } void onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures.set(0); } boolean allowRequest(long now) { long opened = openedAtMillis; // 5. read the volatile once return opened == 0 || now - opened > 30_000; } }

alt.html: class IssuerBreaker { private val consecutiveFailures = AtomicInteger() // 1. many writers: atomic @Volatile private var openedAtMillis = 0L // 2. readers need one value: @Volatile fun onFailure(now: Long) { val n = consecutiveFailures.incrementAndGet() // 3. one atomic step, and keep the result if (n == 5) openedAtMillis = now // 4. only one thread sees n == 5 } fun onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures.set(0) } fun allowRequest(now: Long): Boolean { val opened = openedAtMillis // 5. read the volatile once return opened == 0L || now - opened > 30_000 } }

steps.say: Two habits made this work. Use the value the atomic call returns: calling incrementAndGet() and then get() would bring the check-then-act gap back. And read a volatile into a local once when you use it twice, as allowRequest does, so both uses see the same value. When the breaker grows a half-open state that must let exactly one trial request through while it also resets the counter, two fields change together, and that is the point to switch to a lock.

lab.title: Choose volatile, atomic or lock for a payment session
steps: Run the tests once. Four of the five fail: two waiters never see a write, the attempt counter comes up short, and the money invariant breaks.
Try the quick fix first: put volatile on every field and run the tests. Two still fail. Before reading on, say which two and why.
Now go field by field. Read the comment that says who writes it and who reads it, choose volatile, an atomic or a lock, and add a one-line comment saying why.
Keep every public signature as it is. Run the tests until all five pass, then twice more.
hints: status and lastHeartbeatMillis each have one writer, and the new value doesn't depend on the old one.
attempts++ is read-modify-write with many writers. An AtomicInteger lets attempts() keep returning int.
tryRefund reads capturedCents, which tryCapture writes. Guard both fields with one lock, and take it in the two getters too. A pair of AtomicLongs can't keep refunded <= captured.
lab.done: All five tests in PaymentSessionTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A gauge and a counter from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write two small classes. KafkaLagGauge: one poller thread calls update(long), metrics threads call lag(). RetryCounter: many threads call onRetry(), a metrics thread calls retries(). Use the lightest correct tool for each, and say in a comment why.

answer.html: // one writer, readers need the latest value: volatile is enough public final class KafkaLagGauge { private volatile long lag; // volatile also keeps the 64-bit write in one piece public void update(long newLag) { lag = newLag; } public long lag() { return lag; } } // many writers doing read-modify-write: atomic (LongAdder if it is very hot) public final class RetryCounter { private final AtomicLong count = new AtomicLong(); public void onRetry() { count.incrementAndGet(); } public long retries() { return count.get(); } }

alt.html: // one writer, readers need the latest value: @Volatile is enough class KafkaLagGauge { @Volatile private var current = 0L // also keeps the 64-bit write in one piece fun update(newLag: Long) { current = newLag } fun lag(): Long = current } // many writers doing read-modify-write: atomic (LongAdder if it is very hot) class RetryCounter { private val count = AtomicLong() fun onRetry() { count.incrementAndGet() } fun retries(): Long = count.get() }

recap: volatile gives visibility (fresh reads, visible writes), ordering (release on write, acquire on read) and one global order of all volatile accesses.
It does not join a read and a write into one step: count++, check-then-act and max = Math.max(max, x) all still race.
Use volatile for one-writer values, flags, timestamps and references to immutable snapshots. Use atomics for one variable with many writers, and a lock when a rule spans several fields.
Ordering only helps threads that both use the volatile: one volatile field doesn't fix a two-thread protocol.
Non-volatile long and double may tear under the JLS; volatile ones never do.
A volatile reference or array covers the reference only, not the object or the elements behind it.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "If volatile makes every read and write go to memory, why does volatile int retries; retries++ still lose updates?" Explain in your own words, and say what you would use instead.
explain.answer: Volatile makes each read see the latest value and each write visible, but retries++ is still three steps: read, add one, write. Two threads can both read 41 before either writes, and both write 42. Each access was perfectly volatile; the problem is the gap between them, which volatile doesn't close. For one counter with many writers I'd use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), which does the read and the write as one atomic step, or LongAdder if it's a hot metrics counter. If the update had to touch more than one field, I'd use a lock.

deeper.html:
Atomic classes are volatile fields with extra operations. AtomicInteger.get() and set() have the same memory effects as reading and writing a volatile int. What the class adds is atomic read-modify-write: incrementAndGet, compareAndSet, getAndUpdate, accumulateAndGet. The functional ones (updateAndGet and friends) retry a compare-and-set in a loop, so the function you pass may run more than once and must have no side effects.

Why is the JLS rule for long and double still there, when 64-bit JVMs never tear? Because the JLS is written for every JVM, including 32-bit ones, and dropping the rule would force those JVMs to use more expensive instructions for every 64-bit access. The VarHandle Javadoc states the same rule for its plain mode: plain reads and writes are guaranteed bitwise atomic only for references and for primitive values of 32 bits or less.

A related term you may meet is word tearing: a write to one field or array element changing a neighbor, as some CPUs would do for single bytes. Java forbids it outright. Every field and every array element is its own variable, so a byte[] shared between threads never corrupts the byte next to the one you wrote. Races on that array are still races, of course.
